newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Xmas binge to make UK retailers' profits sparkle.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Xmas binge to make UK retailers' profits sparkle.

text.p: Spending is back in fashion in Britain, making sure the tills will ring merrily this Christmas with shoppers apparently set on a 1980s-style binge.

Sales are already booming because rising incomes and house prices, plus windfall cash from building society flotations, have made people feel richer than for some time. Analysts believe consumer confidence is at its highest since the late 1980s.
"The feelgood factor is out there," said one analyst.

Independent consultants Verdict predict a 7.7 percent increase in spending in December this year over last December, translating into sales of 19.75 billion pounds ($33.16 billion). Official figures show spending is gathering pace. In October retail sales rose 4.1 percent over October last year.
And evidence that inflation is heating up means retailers are probably nudging up margins so most can look forward to a happy new year in profit terms.
"I don't think anyone doubts it's going to be a good Christmas, the question is how good," said John Richards, retail analyst at NatWest Markets.
CHRISTMAS SPENDING STARTED EARLY

In the past people have put off Christmas spending until after the budget in November, but this year they started early, industry sources said. And retailers have stocked up more heavily this year in anticipation of bumper sales.
"Stock markdowns are likely to be a bit lower, the cost outlook is pretty benign, so it's a pretty potent outlook for retailers," said Nick Bubb, analyst at Mees Pierson.
But despite parallels with the shop-till-you-drop 1980s industry watchers are wary of comparing the retail revival to those boom times when consumers spent recklessly and retailers raked in cash.
People are much more choosy and value conscious than they were and retailers have become polarised into the "haves" and "have nots".

"It's not a boom where everyone will do well willy nilly," said Richard Perks of Verdict. "Things are much better than they were last year but this is not an indiscriminate consumer boom by any means," he said.

In clothing, retailers with strong brands -- Next Plc, Marks and Spencer Plc -- will be winners. In durables Argos Plc and electricals retailer Dixons Group Plc will have a cheery festive season, although worries about budget tax changes have hit Dixons shares this week.
Christmas is not the season for DIY, but a long awaited housing upturn is likely to boost Kingfisher Plc's B&Q home improvement stores.
Carpets, DIY, computers, plus the usual favourites toys, clothes and jewellery will all sell well, analysts agreed.

But books and recorded music are not as buoyant, making life tough for W.H. Smith Group Plc, already battling stiff competition on books, videos, CDs and tapes from food superstores like ASDA Group Plc, analysts said.
Others are clearly struggling despite the upturn.

Clothing retailer Country Casuals, for instance, has just issued a profit warning. Department stores group House of Fraser Plc has made losses and Sears Plc, the Selfridges-to-shoes retail empire, has managed to miss the upswing, prompting speculation about a break-up bid or sell-off of its home shopping business Freemans.
But Christmas overall will be good news for retail stocks. "There will be more (profit) upgrades than downgrades," said Richards at NatWest.

The sector has stumbled recently on fears that interest rates will have to rise further to choke off inflation. But analysts said it could regain strength in December/January on the back of firms' Christmas trading statements. ($1=.5956 Pound)
